# The AI-Native Design Life Cycle {#sec-architecture-20-ontology}

::: {.epigraph}
> "All models are wrong but some are useful."
>
> — George E. P. Box, *Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building* [@Box1979Robustness, p. 202]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *Once an AI-native design system is being considered, how should the design work be organized, and why does that structure matter?*

**Core thesis:** *An explicit life cycle connects architectural intent to a reviewed decision. This chapter organizes its responsibilities into six stages (Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit), linked by structured execution records.*
:::

Generative AI models and automated search tools can draft register-transfer level (RTL) code, compiler schedules, and microarchitectural configurations in seconds. When a generator proposes a new neural processing unit (NPU) accumulator organization for our prospective Lighthouse system-on-chip (SoC), however, that speed helps only if the surrounding workflow can compile the proposal, simulate it, check its physical implementation, and trace any failure back to the design choice that caused it without losing track of which candidate produced which numbers. The six-stage life cycle in @fig-ch03-cover-map organizes that work from defining the baseline and physical constraints to deciding what the measured results justify doing next.

Keeping those stages distinct makes it clear what was assumed, what actually ran, and what the tools measured, so a failed check points back to the specific assumption or artifact that needs repair before the error propagates downstream. To see why those boundaries matter, we first examine what breaks when a team connects a generative model directly to simulation and synthesis tools without them, and then follow the Lighthouse NPU accumulator from its initial throughput target through physical timing signoff.

![**Six life-cycle stages connect architectural intent to a reviewed decision through explicit handoffs.** Each stage produces a distinct deliverable: a scoped plan, legal candidates, an execution record, a checked comparison, a supported causal account, and a decision to advance, revise, reject, or stop. Targeted repair routes any failure back to the stage that owns the broken assumption or artifact without discarding valid earlier work.](images/ch03-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch03-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which six life-cycle activities run from formulation through review and decision. Feedback returns work to earlier activities for investigation and revision."}

## What Breaks Without a Structured Life Cycle {#sec-unstructured-loop-failures}

When a team first brings a generative AI model or search algorithm into hardware development, the most tempting setup is an unscripted loop: prompt the model for an RTL block or parameter change, run a simulator or synthesis script, and feed any error log straight back into the prompt until the script exits cleanly. On a standalone arithmetic kernel, that informal cycle feels responsive. On a real subsystem under tight power and timing budgets, running without explicit boundaries between problem definition, exploration, implementation, and evaluation quickly turns rapid iteration into compounding confusion.

The first casualty of an unstructured loop is the baseline itself. When a candidate NPU accumulator misses its throughput or clock target after several automated edits, an unconstrained workflow has no rule separating fixed problem assumptions from choices the generator is free to vary. Across successive retries, a language model or engineer can quietly alter the workload trace, relax a pipeline latency target, or swap a cycle-accurate memory model for an idealized zero-delay stub just to get a clean run. After a few dozen iterations, the loop is still producing latency and area tables, but no one can tell whether the latest candidate is genuinely faster than the original baseline or merely evaluated under softer conditions.

Even when the workload stays fixed, coupling generation directly to evaluation lets an automated loop silence a failing check rather than fix the hardware. If a proposed crossbar organization fails timing analysis or triggers a testbench assertion, an automated agent with write access to the run directory can satisfy its immediate prompt by widening the clock period in the timing-constraint file, marking the critical path as a false path, or weakening the testbench check. The tool script returns zero errors, yet the underlying silicon violation remains untouched.

Finally, when every failed run feeds into the same generic retry prompt, downstream tool queues fill with unexamined candidates while diagnostic costs multiply. Whereas a lint or synthesis error points directly to the offending RTL line, a setup violation found at timing signoff arrives as a failing path through a gate-level netlist, evaluated with extracted wire resistance and capacitance across several process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners far from the architectural choice that produced it. That shortfall might stem from an unrealistic clock target set at the start of the study, a wide crossbar topology that cannot route cleanly, or a misconfigured analysis script, and each cause calls for a different repair. Without stage boundaries that keep those possibilities distinct, an automated loop blindly generates and launches new RTL variants into multi-hour physical implementation runs when the real fix was to revise an upstream assumption or repair a broken script.

## The Six Stages of the AI-Native Life Cycle {#sec-arch2-ontology}

Preventing those compounding failures requires organizing the path from an initial design idea to an engineering commitment so that what the team learns in one step directly informs the others without corrupting the baseline. Separating requirements, design alternatives, implementation, and verification has deep roots in systems engineering, where these activities remain iterative and interdependent [@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook, chap. 4]. Rather than prescribing six separate teams, six software modules, or six rigid steps in a batch flow, the six stages used here organize recurring architecture work so an engineer can follow a candidate design, see what its measurements actually establish, and identify what needs to change when a check fails.

Existing project milestones such as RTL freeze and timing signoff remain in place; the six stages describe the design work that recurs before and between them. Because each stage defines a clear job and the assumptions or artifacts it owns, a failing timing check no longer triggers a blind retry; instead, the team can determine whether to reopen the clock target in Formulate, revise the microarchitecture in Explore, or fix the tool setup in Implement without discarding valid intermediate work.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Isolate failure domains for repair"}
**The principle:** Separate design activities so that a failed result can be traced to the assumptions, artifacts, or checks that need revision.

**The application:** Use the available diagnostics to choose what to revisit, preserving earlier work whose assumptions still hold. When the cause is uncertain or spans several activities, investigate it before choosing a repair.
:::

Each stage answers a question that the next activity depends on:

1. **Formulate.** What should the design achieve? State the question, baseline, constraints, permitted changes, and checks that will judge the result.
2. **Explore.** What alternatives are worth testing? Generate or select candidates, including different hardware and software organizations when the question permits them.
3. **Implement.** How can each candidate be tested? Develop the required models, RTL, and software, and run the tools needed to examine them.
4. **Evaluate.** What do the results establish? Check that the observations are valid for the intended comparison, then determine which requirements are satisfied or still unresolved.
5. **Interpret.** Why did the design behave this way? Test explanations for gains and failures, and use what is learned to guide further design work.
6. **Commit.** What should happen next? Review the study and decide whether to advance a candidate, reject it, revise the study, or stop.

The operational layers defined in @sec-three-operational-layers determine which transitions across these six stages may run automatically. In a Layer 1 workflow, a model helps with bounded tasks such as drafting an isolated block during Implement or summarizing a timing report during Interpret, while engineers coordinate integration, clock-domain crossing (CDC) checks, and repair. A Layer 2 workflow goes further by fixing a structural container $\Theta$ in Formulate so an optimizer can search parameters $\theta \in \Theta$ automatically across Explore, Implement, and Evaluate, handing the problem back to the architect whenever a repair would alter a frozen interface or topology. A Layer 3 system would be permitted to carry physical feedback back into Explore and Implement to revise hardware organization and software together, although whether that broader cross-layer capability (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect) can operate reliably and at lower total cost than a conventional team remains an open question. Across all three layers, prediction, generation, and optimization act as methods invoked inside individual stages rather than separate stages of their own.

Suppose one candidate Lighthouse design uses an NPU for part of its extended reality (XR) workload, one of the compute options left open in @sec-moonshot. Focusing on the accumulator block that combines partial products into matrix-multiplication results, our walkthrough asks how to improve throughput within the block's allocated timing and power limits in a 3\ nm-class design flow. Although the candidates, timing failure, and diagnosis are constructed teaching examples, following this single block through @fig-ontology-loop shows how the six stages and their return paths operate inside a concrete investigation.

![**A scoped architecture study closes the loop only when empirical results drive the next action.** Forward execution steps from declaring the study plan and stopping conditions (Stage 1) through candidate generation, tool execution, measurement validation, and causal testing to a reviewed decision (Stages 2–6). When signoff evidence shows that the original targets or constraints cannot be met within the current scope, the return path from Commit reopens Formulate to revise the study plan.](images/fig-ontology-loop){#fig-ontology-loop width="80%" fig-alt="Life-cycle diagram of six stages arranged in two rows, with arrows from Formulate through Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, to Commit. One return arrow leads from the decision back to formulation."}

Applying the life cycle to a bounded architecture question like the NPU accumulator defines a *scoped study* that investigates one part of the machine without claiming to settle the whole processor. Within that study, a genuine design loop occurs only when an empirical measurement changes the candidate microarchitecture or the study plan and triggers a new action, as defined in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales; running a predetermined parameter grid from start to finish without adapting to the results is a batch sweep, not a design loop.

Scoped studies also depend on one another across hierarchy levels. A subsystem study sets the NPU block's power and timing allocations within the Lighthouse subsystem's 3\ W envelope, while the block study tests whether those allocations can sustain a viable accumulator organization. If no legal candidate closes timing, that shortfall routes back up to re-evaluate the subsystem contract. The walkthrough traces this block study through all six stages before examining how to coordinate multiple coupled studies.

### Stage 1: Formulating the Architecture Question

If a team sets out to "improve NPU accumulator throughput" without first locking down baseline memory assumptions and interface rules, an automated search can spend days optimizing an apparent accumulator bottleneck that vanishes once realistic bus contention is included, or proposing a wider interface that breaks the surrounding SoC contract. Formulation prevents those wasted runs by turning a broad product goal into a testable comparison against an explicit baseline. For the NPU block, the question becomes concrete: can an alternative organization process more matrix-multiplication results per unit time than the baseline accumulator while meeting the target clock period, required numerical behavior, and allocated area and power budgets within the Lighthouse subsystem's 3\ W envelope? Answering that question reliably requires stating the reference design, workload phases, memory and tool assumptions, and verification checks up front while separating fixed system contracts from the choices the study is free to vary.

That boundary between fixed contracts and open choices also defines how far automated repair may reach. In the NPU accumulator walkthrough, the study may modify the internal datapath organization, pipeline structure, and supporting software schedule while holding external bus interfaces and numerical accuracy fixed; if downstream physical checks show that the bus protocol itself limits throughput, the repair loop cannot alter that protocol on its own and must return the question to the architect. Together with an explicit run budget and stopping criteria, these rules yield a testable question and an execution plan against which Explore can propose candidates.

### Stage 2: Exploring Candidate Designs

Once Formulate establishes the question and permitted changes, exploration develops candidate designs worth implementing. While a parameter sweep inside a fixed container can adjust queue depths or clock multipliers around a centralized crossbar using cycle-level simulators or fast analytical surrogates, it cannot alter the crossbar topology itself. Proposing a structural alternative steps outside that container: a generator might replace the centralized crossbar with distributed accumulator banks and local reduction trees, a hardware change that works only when paired with a compiler lowering schedule and tile-movement pattern matched to the new bank layout.

These alternatives trade off more than raw throughput. Adding parallel datapaths consumes extra storage and routing tracks, whereas banking shortens critical interconnect wires at the cost of potential bank conflicts or extra reduction stages. Exploration surfaces these trade-offs and selects informative candidates to test rather than certifying physical feasibility from a high-level model. A cycle simulator that omits interconnect wire delay[^fn-wire-delay-c03] can easily overstate the throughput of a wider centralized crossbar because it ignores the physical resistance and capacitance of long wires. Any search guided solely by such surrogates can propose designs that look optimal in simulation yet fail timing signoff, which is why the life cycle preserves a return path from physical evaluation back to exploration for parameter and topology changes alike.

[^fn-wire-delay-c03]: **Interconnect wire delay**: In advanced nanoscale fabrication nodes, wire resistance and parasitic capacitance scale unfavorably compared to transistor gate delays. Depending on wire length and the target clock period, long interconnect wires across wide crossbars may need repeater buffers or pipelined traversal. A model that assumes single-cycle communication can then overestimate the implementation's throughput.

How a team searches those trade-offs depends on what limits the study. When only a few accumulator organizations are on the table, implementing and comparing them directly is often the cheapest path; when the candidate space grows larger, predictive models can screen out weak designs, optimizers can ration scarce tool runs, and generators can propose new topologies. Because each method introduces its own setup cost and modeling assumptions, the practical test is whether it helps answer the architectural comparison within the available budget (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).

```{python}
#| echo: false
import csv as _csv3ka
import json as _json3ka
from pathlib import Path as _Path3ka
import _python.plots as _ap3ka

_ka10_dir = _Path3ka(_ap3ka.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data" / "studies" / "10-kernelagent-search"
_ka10_sum = {r["label"]: r for r in _json3ka.loads((_ka10_dir / "summary.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))}
_ka10_rows = list(_csv3ka.DictReader((_ka10_dir / "timings.csv").open(encoding="utf-8")))
_ka10_mv_r5 = next(
    float(r["time_ms"])
    for r in _ka10_rows
    if r["label"] == "Matrix–vector" and int(r["round"]) == 5
)
ka10_tasks = len(_ka10_sum)
ka10_rounds = max(int(r["round"]) for r in _ka10_rows)
ka10_total = len(_ka10_rows)
ka10_mv_first = f"{_ka10_sum['Matrix–vector']['first_ms']:.2f}"
ka10_mv_best = f"{_ka10_sum['Matrix–vector']['best_ms']:.2f}"
ka10_mv_ratio = f"{_ka10_sum['Matrix–vector']['first_over_best']:.2f}"
ka10_mv_regress_rounds = _ka10_sum["Matrix–vector"]["rounds_above_previous_best"]
ka10_mv_r5 = f"{_ka10_mv_r5:.2f}"
ka10_rms_first = f"{_ka10_sum['RMSNorm']['first_ms']:.2f}"
ka10_rms_best = f"{_ka10_sum['RMSNorm']['best_ms']:.2f}"

```

Throughout this search, the exploration history records why each candidate was selected or set aside. Proposals that violate a frozen interface can be rejected immediately, whereas a candidate with uncertain timing may still merit implementation if it tests a useful microarchitectural hypothesis. Even in bounded automated kernel tuning, individual search rounds frequently regress against the best candidate found so far before a later round improves the frontier (@fig-ch03-kernelagent-search-trajectories).

![**Automated kernel exploration advances through non-monotonic candidate trials.** Two-panel trace across `{python} ka10_tasks` curated KernelBench operators over `{python} ka10_rounds` rounds (`{python} ka10_total` retained records, one worker per round from a four-worker beam search) [@Cheng2025KernelAgentArtifacts]: (a) matrix–vector multiplication per-round latency (dashed orange line) and best-so-far frontier (solid green step curve), improving `{python} ka10_mv_ratio`$\times$ from Round 1 to Round 8 despite `{python} ka10_mv_regress_rounds` slower intermediate rounds; and (b) best-retained latency relative to Round 1 (solid step curves), where RMSNorm stays nearly flat (`{python} ka10_rms_ratio`$\times$).](images/fig-ch03-kernelagent-search-trajectories){#fig-ch03-kernelagent-search-trajectories width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel line chart across eight optimization rounds for five curated KernelBench operators. Panel (a) plots matrix-vector multiplication latency in milliseconds, where a dashed orange line shows non-monotonic per-round candidate latency with five intermediate regressions and a solid green step curve traces the monotonic best-retained frontier. Panel (b) plots best-retained latency as a fraction of Round 1 across all five operators using solid step curves with markers."}

In the `{python} ka10_tasks` published eight-round traces from @Cheng2025KernelAgentArtifacts, matrix–vector multiplication drops from `{python} ka10_mv_first`\ ms in Round 1 to `{python} ka10_mv_best`\ ms in Round 8 (`{python} ka10_mv_ratio`$\times$), yet `{python} ka10_mv_regress_rounds` of the seven follow-up rounds run slower than the previous best retained candidate, including an `{python} ka10_mv_r5`\ ms regression at Round 5. Across the same eight-round budget, RMSNorm changes only from `{python} ka10_rms_first`\ ms to `{python} ka10_rms_best`\ ms (`{python} ka10_rms_ratio`$\times$). Because these five tasks are author-selected workspace traces rather than a representative sample of KernelBench, they do not establish a general speedup distribution; what they show is why the exploration record must keep every candidate trial distinct from the retained frontier instead of overwriting earlier rounds in place. While changes permitted by the study plan proceed directly to Implement, any proposal that requires altering a system interface or power allocation routes back to Formulate for scope review.

### Stage 3: Implementing Testable Hardware and Software

A promising banked accumulator proposal is useless in practice if its compiled software schedule still routes matrix tiles for a centralized crossbar, or if a misconfigured build script tests the new RTL against stale transaction models. Stage 3 (Implement) turns an abstract candidate from Explore into synchronized hardware, software, and verification inputs that tools can actually execute. For the banked NPU alternative, implementation produces transaction-level models of data movement, synthesizable RTL for the distributed accumulator banks, and a compiler schedule matched to the new bank layout. To keep generation and verification independent (@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales), the team checks these artifacts against a reference fixed before the candidate was generated, such as formal property assertions or a golden model, before spending downstream tool budget.

Building those hardware and software artifacts is only half of implementation; the study also has to run them through tools that match the fidelity of the question. An early behavioral model is enough to test an algorithm or tiling schedule, whereas estimating physical timing requires synthesizable RTL and calibrated electrical models, raising the representation choices developed in @sec-data-representations-world-models. Open research flows such as OpenROAD Flow Scripts make electronic design automation (EDA) steps such as logic synthesis, placement, and routing scriptable on open process nodes [@OpenROADDocs], but commercial 3\ nm-class tapeouts depend on proprietary foundry-qualified design rule decks and signoff engines whose license limits and multi-hour runtimes restrict how many candidates a team can run through physical implementation at once.

Because verification cost rises sharply from fast syntax linting and functional simulation to full synthesis, place-and-route, and timing runs, teams screen candidates in tiers, rejecting flawed designs with cheap checks before spending scarce physical-implementation cycles. Tiered screening saves compute, however, only when each early check is treated as a filter rather than a signoff certificate: passing a behavioral simulation justifies running synthesis on a candidate, but says nothing about whether the resulting layout will satisfy the foundry's physical design rules.[^fn-drc-c03]

[^fn-drc-c03]: **Design rule checking (DRC)**: A check of layout geometry against a semiconductor foundry's manufacturing rules, such as minimum wire widths and spacing. Passing establishes compliance with the rules checked rather than guaranteed fabrication yield, and behavioral simulation never tests these geometric limits.

Even before physical checks begin, implementation has to verify that the tools actually tested the intended design. A syntactically clean script can still point to the wrong top-level module, hold an active-low reset asserted throughout simulation, or skip the target workload phase; similarly, a generated RTL block can pass its unit testbench while violating an interconnect handshake, omitting power-domain isolation cells,[^fn-power-domain-isolation-c03] or compiling against a mismatched software target. The execution harness prevents those silent mismatches by keeping the candidate hardware, supporting software, interface assertions, and tool inputs tied together throughout the run.

[^fn-power-domain-isolation-c03]: **Power-domain isolation**: Specialized clamp circuits placed at boundaries between independent voltage or power domains on an SoC. When a block is powered off to eliminate static leakage, isolation cells hold boundary signals at defined logic levels (0 or 1) to prevent floating inputs and destructive short-circuit crowbar currents in neighboring active blocks.

When a tool run fails outright, the harness must also separate operational faults from bad hardware before feeding the outcome back into search. A license checkout timeout says nothing about circuit timing, and a host out-of-memory kill might reflect a cramped container limit, a tool bug, or a genuinely unroutable netlist. Tracking those distinctions across automated retries is the job of the tool interfaces and run management developed in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces; once a run completes cleanly, Stage 4 (Evaluate) asks what the returned measurements actually establish about the design.

### Stage 4: Evaluating Candidates with Simulators and Tools

Once implementation confirms that the intended design and workload actually ran, evaluation checks whether the returned measurements answer the planned question, since a clean tool exit alone does not make a measurement valid. A loop that relies on fast surrogates and cycle-level simulators to evaluate many candidates cheaply can easily overrate designs whose delay is dominated by global wiring. To establish the NPU candidate's physical and functional feasibility, evaluation requires checks that can observe those implementation limits directly, including static timing analysis (STA),[^fn-sta-c03] design rule checking (DRC), logic equivalence checking, CDC checks, and dynamic voltage-drop ($IR$-drop) analysis. Any study that stops short of those checks must keep its conclusions within the models it actually ran.

Suppose a candidate with a wider centralized crossbar compiles cleanly and a C++ cycle simulator predicts higher accumulator throughput at the target clock frequency. If STA then reports a setup timing violation on the accumulator paths while power-integrity analysis flags localized $IR$-drop near critical buffers,[^fn-ir-drop-c03] evaluation records that the design fails its declared timing constraint. Because the simulated throughput gain assumes a clock frequency that the physical layout cannot sustain, the candidate cannot be accepted as an improvement.

[^fn-sta-c03]: **Static timing analysis (STA)**: An exhaustive verification method that calculates signal propagation delays across all circuit paths against clock constraints without dynamic simulation vectors. A setup timing violation indicates negative slack, meaning data arrives too late relative to the clock edge and the circuit cannot reliably operate at the target clock frequency.

[^fn-ir-drop-c03]: **IR drop**: A voltage decrease caused by current flowing through resistance in the power-distribution network. Reduced supply voltage can slow switching and contribute to timing violations.

Evaluation records each requirement separately as passed, failed, or unresolved, so a passing functional test does not mask a timing violation and an unmeasured power budget remains marked as unknown. While the localized voltage drop offers an initial clue to why the paths slowed down, evaluation only registers which constraints passed or failed; determining the physical cause of the failure is the job of Interpret.

### Stage 5: Interpreting What the Measurements Show

Knowing which checks passed or failed does not by itself tell the team what to change next, because the same measured gain or timing violation can arise from several different mechanisms. In the NPU study, the architect must distinguish a long crossbar wire path from inadequate power delivery, weak buffer sizing, or an improperly configured timing constraint, and Stage 5 asks which explanation the evidence supports and what test would separate the remaining possibilities. Mapping this diagnosis onto the three operational layers shows how far each workflow's automated repair loop can reach and where it must hand the problem back to people.

At Layer 1, a model can help inspect a timing report or rewrite an arithmetic expression inside a single module, using a floorplan or clock-tree log as context without having authority to coordinate a structural repair. The engineer weighs the diagnosis, chooses the fix, and carries it through integration and verification.

Moving to a Layer 2 workflow automates local repair by adjusting parameters $\theta$ within the fixed hardware container $\Theta$. When a path misses timing, the optimizer can try permitted physical fixes such as gate sizing, swapping in lower-threshold-voltage ($V_t$) cells, inserting buffers, or tuning useful clock skew. In leading-edge FinFET and nanosheet nodes (such as 3\ nm), however, aggressive $V_t$ swapping raises subthreshold leakage exponentially ($I_{\text{sub}} \propto e^{-qV_t / (n k T)}$, with $n$ the subthreshold slope factor), which can quickly consume the block's share of the prospective 3\ W envelope. Once those local repairs fail to close timing within the leakage limit because the critical paths cross the centralized crossbar, the next step is to inspect the failing paths and test whether interconnect delay explains the shortfall. If that diagnosis points to a crossbar redesign that would alter a frozen bus contract or memory organization, the optimizer must pause and request architectural review to reopen Formulate.

A Layer 3 workflow would go further by carrying physical signoff diagnostics across life-cycle and abstraction boundaries. When timing analysis reports that net delay dominates cell delay across the centralized crossbar, such a system would not stop at local cell swaps or relaxing the clock target; it could return to Stage 2 (Explore) to propose distributed accumulator banks, advance to Stage 3 (Implement) to build local reduction trees with a matching compiler schedule, and rerun physical signoff to test whether the new organization actually closes timing.

Across any of these workflows, deciding whether to redesign the crossbar requires testing the diagnosis itself rather than acting on the first plausible story. Automated tools can assist this interpretation by extracting critical timing paths, comparing cell-delay and net-delay ratios, and proposing candidate explanations.[^fn-credit-assignment-c03] Isolating the contribution of wire delay, however, requires running a controlled counterfactual through Implement and Evaluate, such as testing a shorter interconnect path or local retiming under identical analysis settings while checking whether accompanying shifts in buffering, placement, or capacitive load confound the result. That diagnostic work needs its own run budget so troubleshooting experiments cannot quietly consume the study's overall search allocation.

If the counterfactual evidence confirms that long shared global interconnect is the limiting factor, the next iteration can test the distributed-bank alternative under the same physical signoff checks, whether a Layer 3 system or an architect proposes it. Deciding which observations justify a structural redesign, and which explanations still need testing, connects this stage to the verification and feedback methods developed in @sec-feedback-verification-trust.

[^fn-credit-assignment-c03]: **The architectural credit assignment problem**: In multi-stage closed-loop design, attributing a downstream physical failure (such as negative slack, routing congestion, or localized $IR$-drop) to an upstream design decision is a classic credit assignment challenge. A timing violation could originate from an over-aggressive clock constraint in Formulate, a poor microarchitectural topology in Explore, awkward coding style in Implement, or suboptimal seed initialization in physical synthesis. Sensitivity analysis and controlled counterfactual trials can help distinguish these causes before triggering expensive structural redesigns.

Because a generated explanation remains an unverified hypothesis until controlled observations distinguish it from competing causes, automated diagnosis is a capability that must be tested within the study's scope. When the available runs cannot isolate a single root cause, the study retains the competing explanations and either requests further diagnostic runs or moves to Commit for review, treating a clear account of what remains unresolved as a useful engineering outcome alongside a supported design recommendation.

### Stage 6: Reviewing the Evidence and Making a Decision

Without an explicit review step at the end of a study, an automated loop can promote a block whose local speedup shifts memory traffic and thermal load onto neighboring SoC blocks, or mistake an exhausted run budget for proof that a target is infeasible. Commit prevents both errors by bringing the study to a reviewed decision on what the completed work justifies doing next: advancing a candidate, rejecting it, revising the question, or stopping with unresolved issues. Because the stakes depend on the study's scope, advancing a revised NPU block to subsystem integration carries different obligations from approving a full chip for mask freeze.[^fn-mask-freeze-c03] When a revised NPU block satisfies its declared checks, the responsible architect reviews the hardware and software changes, the comparison conditions, the physical explanation for the speedup, and the remaining system-level limitations before recommending integration. If timing still fails or the run budget runs out, the architect can authorize another study or record that the bounded search ended without a winner.

[^fn-mask-freeze-c03]: **Mask freeze**: The final signoff milestone (often termed tapeout) where physical layout geometries are locked and released to manufacture optical lithography reticles (photomasks). Unlike a software patch, a silicon defect found after mask freeze generally requires new masks and a respin, which at advanced process nodes is among the most expensive and time-consuming corrections a program can make.

This division of labor lets automated loops do useful work inside the scope and budget set during Formulate without turning every tool invocation into a separate manual approval. Routine implementation and tuning iterations proceed automatically, while human review is reserved for when a candidate meets the planned decision criteria, when a repair requires changing the study's scope, or when a stopping condition triggers.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="From the NPU block to the Lighthouse subsystem"}
**Context.** The accumulator study examines one block in a candidate Lighthouse design. Its results must eventually be evaluated in the XR workload that motivated the design.

**Application.** Faster accumulation may shorten a workload stage, but additional transfers or memory contention may erase that gain. The integrated comparison must check workload deadlines, the matching software schedule, and power across the subsystem, including memory and leakage.

**Outcome.** A successful block study could justify evaluating the revised NPU in the surrounding system. Whether that Lighthouse candidate meets its 3\ W target and real-time requirements remains a question for the subsystem study.
:::

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Stop when the tools cannot observe the target"}
**The principle:** A valid architectural outcome includes rejecting every candidate, retaining the baseline reference, or halting exploration before tool dispatch when available tools cannot observe target physical reality.

**The application:** An analytical memory model such as CACTI derives its estimates from generic technology parameters, not from a leading-edge foundry's qualified bitcells, multi-threshold leakage distributions, or write-assist circuits, so at a node such as TSMC N3E its numbers are uncalibrated estimates rather than signoff-grade results. When evaluation prerequisites or calibrated tool collateral are missing, an AI-native design system should stop before dispatch, or label the returns as uncalibrated, rather than treat them as measurements. Stopping there is a valid outcome of the study, and its record should state what was missing.
:::

Together, the six stages serve as a practical reference for planning and reviewing a study, keeping their starting inputs, deliverables, and return conditions distinct even when one engineer or tool performs several activities (@tbl-stage-seams).

| **Stage** | **Starts from** | **Produces** | **Reason to revisit** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Formulate** | Product goals and system requirements. | A question, baseline, scope, checks, and stopping conditions. | Evidence calls the target, assumptions, or permitted changes into question. |
| **Explore** | The plan and what earlier candidates taught. | Candidate organizations or configurations, with reasons for testing them. | A candidate fails, or a result suggests a better alternative. |
| **Implement** | A candidate and the checks it needs. | Testable hardware and software, tool inputs, and execution results. | Artifacts need revision, or the intended checks did not run. |
| **Evaluate** | Execution results and the planned comparison. | Valid comparisons and passed, failed, or unresolved checks. | Conditions are mismatched or observations are insufficient. |
| **Interpret** | Checked results and possible explanations. | Supported explanations, remaining hypotheses, and proposed investigations. | Causes remain uncertain or another result contradicts the explanation. |
| **Commit** | The plan, comparisons, explanations, and limitations. | A reviewed decision to advance, reject, revise, or stop. | Missing evidence or a changed requirement reopens the decision. |
: **Inputs, outputs, and return conditions across the six life-cycle stages.** Each stage owns a distinct engineering deliverable and reopens when downstream measurements invalidate its starting assumptions or artifacts. {#tbl-stage-seams tbl-colwidths="[15,25,30,30]"}

The dependencies across @tbl-stage-seams also make clear that no stage operates on the output of its immediate predecessor alone: Evaluate compares the raw results from Implement against the criteria fixed in Formulate, and Commit weighs the accumulated baselines, failed trials, and causal explanations rather than only the final run. Those same stage boundaries mark how far a workflow's repair loop may reach when a check fails and when the problem must route back to Formulate to reconsider the targets or stop without a candidate. Because an automated search can execute dozens of iterations before an architect reviews the outcome, the workflow needs a structured way to record those connections so another architect can follow what happened, which operational layer governed the search, and why a specific repair was chosen.

## Recording the Loop in a Study Record {#sec-design-loop-card}

Reviewing the NPU study requires more than its best timing report. Another architect needs to know which candidate produced that report, which workload and constraints applied, why the candidate was selected, and what earlier failures taught the team. Much of this information already sits in repositories, experiment logs, and verification reports, but scattered files do not explain a design choice until they are connected to the original question and the resulting decision.

A *study record* provides that connected account by linking the initial plan, candidate revisions, comparisons, explanations, and failed or unfinished runs to the final decision or stopping reason. An *execution record*, by contrast, captures a single tool attempt, including its inputs, random seeds when applicable, library versions, tool environment, diagnostic outputs, and completion status. In the NPU example, one execution record logs the setup timing violation on the centralized accumulator, while the study record explains how that failure led the team to test a banked accumulator design. Keeping both levels intact means saving every failed run and recording what changed on a retry, rather than overwriting a shared scratch directory and erasing the history needed to explain why the design moved.

> **Design-loop card.** A short structured index, fixed before any tool runs, that records a scoped study's baseline, candidate space, execution budget, verification criteria, and reviewer, and links each later execution record back to that plan [@MitchellEtAl2019ModelCards; @GebruEtAl2021Datasheets]. It borrows contextual documentation from Model Cards and Datasheets for Datasets and points into existing engineering records rather than replacing them.

Placing a scoped study record between high-level design intent and individual tool invocations keeps the engineering rationale attached to the files that test it (@fig-structured-layer-above-rtl). Rather than imposing a heavy software framework, this intermediate layer simply records which questions, constraints, and tool runs depend on one another.

![**A scoped architecture study links high-level design judgment to low-level tool execution.** Top-level design intent, analytical models, and system requirements feed into a bounded study record that tracks the question under review, linked artifacts, and supported findings. Below it, outputs from simulators, compilers, RTL generators, and EDA signoff engines return along a common path to either support an architectural decision or trigger a claim revision.](images/fig-structured-layer-above-rtl){#fig-structured-layer-above-rtl width="72%" fig-alt="Diagram in which system intent and human judgment appear above a scoped architecture study, which links its question and artifacts to results from implementation tools below. Feedback connects the study to further design work and review."}

Without those links, a raw cycle count tells a reviewer nothing unless they also know the workload trace that drove it and the simulator configuration that produced it. A physical timing estimate likewise means little without the applicable PVT corners,[^fn-pvt-c03] calibrated cell libraries, and clock constraints specified in Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) files.[^fn-sdc-c03] Tying each tool output back to the study card lets a reviewer distinguish an early simulated cycle speedup from a design that actually passes DRC and STA signoff, and shows immediately which comparisons must be rerun when an upstream assumption changes.

[^fn-pvt-c03]: **Process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners**: Combinations of device-model and operating assumptions used to check a design under different conditions. The limiting combination can differ across timing and power checks.

[^fn-sdc-c03]: **Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC)**: A format for specifying clocks, input and output delays, timing exceptions, and related constraints used by synthesis and timing-analysis tools.

To see how a second study fits alongside the NPU accumulator investigation within the same Lighthouse design, consider a companion comparison of 2, 3, and 4\ MiB level-2 (L2) cache capacities with all other architectural choices held fixed. Here the question is whether fewer capacity misses reduce frame-time tail latency on the selected XRBench workload while keeping array access time, silicon area, and total power (including static leakage) within the subsystem's 3\ W budget.

Because bus widths, cache-line sizes, replacement policies, and interconnect protocols all remain fixed, this cache comparison sits inside the kind of frozen hardware template that a Layer 2 optimizer would normally search. With only three capacity options, however, the architect needs no learned optimizer and no iterative loop; a direct three-point sweep is enough. Even so, recording the baseline, candidates, physical checks, and signoff criteria on a design-loop card before running any tools keeps this simple sweep just as auditable as a larger automated search.

Evaluating each cache capacity requires two different tools: a cycle-level simulator to measure frame times on the workload trace, and a static random-access memory (SRAM) model[^fn-sram-model-c03] to estimate the memory array's area, access latency, and dynamic and leakage power. Checking whether the subsystem stays within its 3\ W envelope also requires accounting for the power drawn by the NPU and surrounding blocks. Because no single tool measures the whole question, the design-loop card serves as the common index that binds the simulator output, the SRAM estimates, and the subsystem power check to the same candidate and workload.

[^fn-sram-model-c03]: **SRAM memory models**: Dense multi-megabyte cache arrays use custom analog-digital bitcells and sense amplifiers that cannot be efficiently synthesized from standard logic gates. Architectural exploration relies on analytical tools (such as CACTI) or foundry memory compilers to evaluate area, access latency, dynamic read and write energy, and static leakage for specific banking configurations.

Expressing that index in a machine-readable format gives both automated search tools and human reviewers the same starting contract before any tool runs (@fig-filled-design-loop-card). Version-controlling the card alongside the repository locks in the baseline, candidate set, execution budget, and rejection criteria up front.

![**A pre-committed design-loop card separates the study plan from its eventual outcome.** For the prospective Lighthouse L2 cache sweep (2, 3, and 4\ MiB), twelve fields record the claim under review, workload state, direct-enumeration method, tool budget, and signoff reviewer before execution begins, leaving the supported-evidence and decision fields open until every check returns.](images/fig-filled-design-loop-card){#fig-filled-design-loop-card width="75%" fig-alt="Illustration of a study card for a prospective XR cache study. A hypothesis precedes entries for the baseline, candidates, checks, execution budget, evidence needed, and responsible reviewer. No completed result is reported."}

The evaluation budget in @fig-filled-design-loop-card caps cycle-level simulation at four runs (one for each of the three capacities plus a single rerun) alongside one SRAM screening evaluation per capacity. That ceiling is deliberately tight because cycle-accurate simulation over long frame traces is slow. If a simulator run aborts on a timeout, or if input-trace variation leaves the 99th-percentile frame time too noisy to separate the candidates within four runs, the architect stops and records the study as unresolved rather than quietly expanding the budget. Keeping the NPU accumulator and L2 cache studies on separate cards isolates their immediate failure domains without hiding their physical coupling: once the team adopts the banked NPU accumulator, its altered interconnect traffic and heat dissipation change the subsystem baseline, prompting the architect to reopen the cache card with updated background power assumptions.

Taken together, the accumulator and cache studies illustrate why an architect must weigh hardware choices and representation limits at the same time. Just as a Layer 2 parameter vector that exposes only buffer sizes cannot represent a banked accumulator even when a generator suggests one, sweeping L2 cache capacity inside a fixed memory hierarchy will eventually plateau once off-chip bandwidth limits the frame rate. Breaking through that bandwidth wall requires changes the cache study's fixed template rules out, such as interconnect compression, new packet formats, or reshaped compiler data layouts. Making those changes requires reformulating the study itself, whether a human architect leads that redesign today or a Layer 3 system eventually proposes it in response to physical signoff feedback.

The chapters that follow build out the technical pieces needed to run and audit this life cycle. Automated methods first need structured ways to represent designs, workloads, and physical constraints (@sec-data-representations-world-models), while the selection criteria in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization show how to match generation, prediction, and optimization techniques to a specific architecture question and run budget. Wrapping simulators and EDA flows into reproducible execution harnesses (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces) then pairs with the verification discipline of @sec-feedback-verification-trust to check what those tools return before any result drives a design change. Because these building blocks support several life-cycle stages at once rather than mapping to the six stages one for one, the closing chapters step back to examine recurring loop patterns across the hardware-software stack (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack), benchmark complete design workflows against simpler baselines in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect, and establish in @sec-what-architect-owns why a human architect remains accountable for the final signoff decision.

## Open Questions

Breaking the design loop into six explicit stages clarifies what each handoff must record, but it also exposes four hard research problems that arise when teams try to automate those handoffs across real hardware tools:

- **How do we filter out weak candidates early without throwing away hardware designs that only work once the compiler schedule and physical layout are tuned to match them?** Running candidates step by step through behavioral simulation, logic synthesis, and place-and-route saves scarce EDA licenses, but strict early cutoffs can reject a promising distributed accumulator simply because it was tested with a compiler schedule built for a centralized crossbar. Computational drug discovery faces the same trap when rigid early docking filters discard novel molecules that bind well only after the target protein relaxes to fit them. Yet the opposite approach, tuning a custom compiler schedule and running physical placement for every proposed block, quickly burns the study's compute budget on designs that fail basic functional or area checks. We still lack multi-stage screening rules that can bound the risk of rejecting a good hardware organization before its software and physical layout have had a chance to adapt.

- **When a post-route signoff check fails, how can an automated workflow tell which earlier stage caused the problem?** When STA or dynamic $IR$-drop signoff fails in a 3\ nm flow, the tool reports a failing gate-level path through extracted wire parasitics. That single violation could come from an unrealistic clock target set in Formulate, a centralized crossbar chosen in Explore, unpipelined RTL written in Implement, or random variation in the placement seed. An architect or automated loop cannot afford to rerun full place-and-route to test every possible explanation, yet blaming wire-dominated delay on local gate sizing will trap a Layer 2 optimizer in pointless $V_t$ swaps. We need diagnostic methods that can pinpoint which upstream stage broke the design using only a handful of targeted tool runs.

- **When an optimizer fails to find a working design, how do we tell whether the search simply ran out of budget or the hardware template itself cannot meet the target?** Suppose a Layer 2 optimizer repeatedly fails to close timing on the NPU accumulator without exceeding the 3\ W subthreshold leakage limit. Those failed runs alone do not prove that no valid parameter setting $\theta$ exists inside the fixed hardware template $\Theta$. If the template truly has no working point, running more parameter sweeps wastes compute; if a valid point is still hiding in the space, reopening Formulate too early to relax the clock target or change bus interfaces lets a weak search algorithm off the hook. We still lack reliable tests that combine physical scaling limits, calibrated surrogate uncertainty, and formal infeasibility bounds to tell an architect when to stop tuning parameters and change the hardware organization.

- **How can separate block-level studies share power, thermal, and bandwidth budgets without forcing the team to optimize the entire SoC at once?** Scoped design-loop cards keep each block's failure modes easy to inspect, but neighboring blocks still share physical budgets: adopting a faster banked NPU accumulator changes bursty interconnect traffic and heat dissipation enough to invalidate a companion L2 cache study inside the same 3\ W envelope. No team can afford to rerun cycle-accurate simulation and full place-and-route across the whole subsystem after every block edit, yet rigid upfront budgets for each block miss cross-block trade-offs. Aerospace engineers face a similar problem in multidisciplinary design optimization, where airframe, propulsion, and flight-control teams coordinate shared weight and drag margins without folding the entire aircraft into a single solver. Hardware design loops need similar ways to pass power, thermal, and bandwidth sensitivities between sibling study cards and flag when two coupled blocks must be optimized together.

## Summary

Whether a team runs a simple parameter sweep or wrestles with those open research problems, the six-stage life cycle connects an architecture question to candidate proposals, testable implementation, valid measurement, causal diagnosis, and a reviewed decision. In our NPU study, a promising throughput estimate led to physical synthesis checks, a setup timing failure, and a structural shift from a centralized accumulator to a banked organization. Progress depended not on any single model or tool, but on passing what each stage learned to the stage that needed it next and looping back to earlier assumptions whenever new evidence required a change.

This shared structure gives the rest of the book a common backbone while leaving room for very different levels of automation. A three-point L2 cache comparison can evaluate every candidate by hand, whereas a broader AI-native study may generate and test new hardware and software organizations automatically. Both studies still require fair comparisons, recorded tool conditions, and an explicit account of what the evidence actually supports; changing how much of the loop is automated never removes those engineering obligations.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Begin with a testable question.** The baseline, requirements, permitted changes, and stopping conditions make later comparisons meaningful while leaving room for alternative organizations.
- **Connect generation to implementation.** A proposed organization needs a representation that can express it, along with matching hardware, software, and checks before its benefits can be assessed.
- **Separate evaluation from interpretation.** Establish what passed, failed, or remains unknown, then investigate why and use the findings to guide another design.
- **Revisit the work affected by a result.** Preserve earlier results whose assumptions still hold, and investigate coupled causes before selecting a repair.
- **Keep the decision proportional to the evidence.** Retain the conditions, failed attempts, and limitations needed for review: advancing, rejecting, revising, and stopping unresolved are all legitimate outcomes, and exhausting a run budget only ends the permitted search rather than proving the target infeasible.
:::

Before any method can propose or compare alternatives like the centralized and banked NPU accumulators, however, it needs a concrete way to encode hardware organizations, workloads, and physical constraints. Turning those design artifacts and tool outputs into machine-usable state is the task of @sec-data-representations-world-models, starting with the architectural data from which every representation and predictive model is built.
